title: Why Reformed call assurance ‘certainty of faith’: it rests partly on a revealed premise, partly on experience
source_text: XXVII. Solenne quidem est Scholae Reformatae Theologis certitudinem fidei vocare, illam qua quis confidit, se esse Deo reconciliatum, & sibi per Christi sanguinem peccata fuisse remissa: sed id ab illis ideo fit quod certitudo illa nitatur altera propositione in verbo Dei revelata, hac scilicet, Quicunque credit in Christum remissionem habet peccatorum in sanguine ejus. Altera vero quae fideli nota est interno sensu & experientia, nempe quod ipse vere credit in Christum, & fiduciam suam in morte illius collocat. Fidelis enim, dum seipsum excutit, & animi sui motus occultos examinat, proculdubio sentire & percipere potest se non ficte in Christum credere, seque Deum serio amare, & illius timore duci; quae vivae fidei sunt signa & τεκμήρια. Hoc autem sufficere putant ut aliquid ad fidei assensum referatur; nimirum, si deducatur ex una propositione quam Deus in Verbo suo revelarit, & ex altera quae experientia, aut alia quadam ratione certa sit. Nec tamen propterea censent quicquid ad fidei assensum refertur, esse ejusdem omnino rationis & necessitatis. Nam ad fidem aliqua ratione pertinet quicquid testimonio divino ullo modo nititur. Sed sunt quaedam quae testimonio divino nituntur in solidum: alia vero quae ex parte quidem divino testimonio; ex parte vero humano sensu, testimonio, vel ratiocinio. Quae autem sunt prioris generis proculdubio majus aliquid habent, quam quae sunt posterioris.
pass_a_gloss: It is indeed customary for theologians of the Reformed school to call that a certainty of faith by which someone trusts that he is reconciled to God and that his sins have been remitted through Christ’s blood; but they do so because that certainty rests on one proposition revealed in God’s word—namely, Whoever believes in Christ has remission of sins in his blood—and on another known to the believer by inward sense and experience, namely that he himself truly believes in Christ and places his trust in Christ’s death. For a believer, examining himself and the hidden motions of his soul, can beyond doubt sense and perceive that he does not fictively believe in Christ, and that he seriously loves God and is led by his fear—which are signs and tokens of living faith. They think this suffices for something to be referred to the assent of faith, namely if it is deduced from one proposition God has revealed in his Word and from another that is certain by experience or some other reason. Yet they do not therefore hold that whatever is referred to the assent of faith is altogether of the same reason and necessity. For whatever rests in any way on divine testimony pertains in some manner to faith. But some things rest wholly on divine testimony; others partly on divine testimony and partly on human sense, testimony, or reasoning. And those of the former kind beyond doubt have something greater than those of the latter.
pass_b_english: Reformed call assurance ‘certainty of faith’ because one premise is revealed and the other is experiential self-knowledge of living faith.
Not everything referred to faith’s assent shares the same necessity as truths resting wholly on divine testimony.
